blocks.text: Memory prompts cover how an agent actually stores and retrieves information across a genuine persistent memory system, beyond the in-conversation context handling covered in the earlier Memory Instructions topic, which was explicitly limited to what is present within a single conversation context window.

This topic covers the difference between working memory within one agent trajectory and long-term memory across sessions, deciding what is genuinely worth storing, prompting the model to query its own memory, and incorporating retrieved memories back into the current prompt without overwhelming it.
1. Memory Prompts vs the Earlier Memory Instructions Topic

blocks.alt: Building on routing prompts, memory prompts cover genuine persistent agent memory

blocks.text: The earlier Memory Instructions topic explicitly stated that genuine persistent memory across separate sessions requires an actual external storage system, memory prompts here cover the prompting side of exactly that system, once it exists, prompting a model to decide what to store and how to use what gets retrieved.

blocks.alt: Memory instructions covered in conversation context only, memory prompts here cover genuine persistent storage

blocks.text: 2. Working Memory vs Long-Term Memory

blocks.alt: Working memory operates within one agent trajectory, long-term memory persists across many separate sessions

blocks.text: Working memory holds information relevant only to the current task in progress, an intermediate result from an earlier step in the same trajectory, long-term memory persists across entirely separate sessions, a user preference or fact learned in one conversation that should still be available days later.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Memory Type","Scope"],"rows":[["Working memory","The current agent trajectory only"],["Long-term memory","Persists across separate future sessions"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Deciding What Is Worth Storing Long-Term

blocks.alt: Every single detail is compared against what is genuinely worth storing long term

blocks.text: Not every detail from a conversation deserves permanent storage, a well designed memory prompt explicitly instructs the model on what genuinely qualifies, a stated user preference, a significant fact, versus what does not, incidental small talk, a one-time detail unlikely to matter again.

code.content:
memory_decision_prompt = (
    "Based on this conversation, identify any facts about the user "
    "that would genuinely be useful to remember in future conversations, "
    "such as stated preferences or important recurring details. "
    "Ignore incidental, one-time details unlikely to matter again."
)

blocks.text: 4. Prompting the Model to Query Its Own Memory

blocks.alt: The model decides to query memory, relevant stored memory gets retrieved, and gets incorporated into the current prompt

blocks.text: This connects directly to the ReAct pattern covered in an earlier module, querying memory is itself an action the model can decide to take, "check memory for anything relevant to this user before responding," the retrieved result then becomes part of the current prompt context, exactly like any other retrieved information.
5. Memory Prompts vs Retrieval Prompting

blocks.alt: Retrieval prompting retrieves from documents, memory prompts retrieve from an agent own past

blocks.text: This connects directly to retrieval prompting, covered in the earlier RAG Prompting module, the underlying mechanics are genuinely similar, querying a store and incorporating what comes back into the prompt, the difference is the source, retrieval typically pulls from external documents, memory pulls from the agent own accumulated history with this user or task.
6. Incorporating Retrieved Memories Into the Current Prompt

Once relevant memory is retrieved, it needs to be clearly delimited within the prompt, exactly like retrieved document content covered in the earlier RAG Prompting module, so the model can distinguish established prior facts about the user from the current conversation content.
7. Avoiding Memory Overload

blocks.alt: Too much retrieved memory crowds out room for the current task

blocks.text: This connects directly to the context window optimization concepts covered in an earlier module, retrieving every single stored memory fact regardless of relevance can crowd out space needed for the actual current task, retrieving only the memories genuinely relevant to the current request keeps this balance reasonable.

blocks.title: This is the same relevance prioritization problem seen elsewhere in this course
blocks.content: Whether the source is a document, a conversation history, or a persistent memory store, the same underlying discipline applies, retrieve and include only what is genuinely relevant to the current need, not everything potentially available.

blocks.text: 8. A Worked Example of Agent Memory Prompting

A personal assistant agent learns in one session that a user prefers concise responses, storing this as a long-term memory fact, in a later, entirely separate session, the agent queries memory at the start, retrieves this stored preference, and incorporates it into its response style for that new conversation, without the user needing to restate it.
9. Memory Prompts and the Separate AI Agents Course

The actual infrastructure behind a persistent memory system, how memories get stored, indexed, and efficiently searched, is covered in much greater technical depth in the separate AI Agents and Tool Calling course, this topic focuses specifically on how to prompt effectively once that underlying system exists.
Worked Example

A team building a coding assistant agent initially has no memory system, users repeatedly need to restate their preferred programming language and coding style conventions in every new session, a genuinely frustrating repetitive experience.

Adding a memory system, with an explicit prompt deciding what preferences are worth storing after each session, and a query step at the start of each new session retrieving relevant stored preferences, eliminates this repetition, the assistant now applies previously stated preferences automatically across separate sessions.
Common Mistakes

items: Storing every incidental detail from a conversation rather than genuinely useful, recurring facts worth remembering
Not clearly delimiting retrieved memory content from the current conversation, causing confusion about what is established versus new
Retrieving too much stored memory at once, crowding out context space needed for the actual current task
Confusing this genuine persistent memory system with the in-conversation context handling covered in the earlier Memory Instructions topic

blocks.text: Practice

Design a memory decision prompt for an agent in a domain you are familiar with, specifying what kinds of facts genuinely deserve long-term storage versus what should be ignored, and sketch how a later session would query and incorporate one of those stored facts.
Key Takeaway

Memory prompts cover deciding what genuinely deserves long-term storage, prompting the model to query its own memory as an explicit action, and incorporating retrieved memories back into the current prompt with the same relevance discipline and clear delimiting used for any other retrieved content, going beyond the in-conversation-only scope covered in the earlier Memory Instructions topic.
